title: Quality Assurance & Peer Review ✅
description: Implement review processes to catch errors, verify findings, and uphold professional standards.

slides.title: Why QA is Non‑Negotiable 🧐
slides.content:
# Mistakes Can Sink a Case

A single error – a wrong timestamp, a miscalculated hash – can destroy your credibility and lead to wrongful outcomes.

Quality Assurance (QA) is a systematic process to:
- Verify technical accuracy.
- Ensure the report meets professional standards.
- Confirm that conclusions are supported by evidence.

Every forensic lab or practitioner should have a QA process.

quizData.question: What is the primary reason for forensic QA?

options.text: To prevent errors and ensure reliability of findings

quizData.explanation: QA safeguards against mistakes that could compromise the investigation and court admissibility.

slides.title: Types of Review 🔍
slides.content:
## Administrative & Technical

- **Administrative Review**: Check for grammar, typos, proper formatting, all required sections present, consistent evidence item numbering.
- **Technical Review**: Another qualified examiner independently verifies:
  - Hash values match.
  - Tool outputs are correctly interpreted.
  - Timestamps are converted correctly.
  - Conclusions logically flow from findings.
- **Peer Review**: A senior or external expert reviews the methodology and conclusions for soundness.

Document the review process: who reviewed, when, and any changes made.

quizData.question: A technical review only needs to check for spelling mistakes.
quizData.explanation: Technical review verifies the accuracy of findings, tool usage, and logical conclusions, not just grammar.

slides.title: Common Errors to Catch 📋
slides.content:
- **Timezone mis‑conversion**: FILETIME to UTC then local – easy to get wrong.
- **Endianness mistakes**: Parsing a FAT entry in wrong byte order.
- **Wrong tool version**: Output from different versions may differ; document the exact version.
- **Orphaned references**: Mentioning an evidence item that doesn't exist.
- **Overstating confidence**: "This proves..." instead of "The evidence indicates..."

A checklist helps avoid these.

slides.title: Sample Verification Checklist
slides.content: A markdown checklist for technical review:
slides.codeSnippet:
- [ ] Source and image hashes verified and match.
- [ ] Tool versions documented.
- [ ] Timestamps converted to correct timezone (specified).
- [ ] All findings linked to evidence items.
- [ ] Conclusions clearly stated as opinion and supported by findings.
- [ ] Acronyms defined on first use.
- [ ] Chain of custody referenced.

quizData.question: Before finalizing a report, an examiner should verify that all timestamps have been correctly converted from ___ to local time.
quizData.explanation: Many file systems store timestamps in UTC; you must convert to the relevant local timezone for the report.

slides.title: Ethics & Professional Standards ⚖️
slides.content:
Follow recognized guidelines:
- **SWGDE** (Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence) – best practices.
- **NIST SP 800‑86** – Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques.
- **ISO/IEC 27037** – Guidelines for digital evidence.

Stay impartial. Do not let the hiring party influence your findings. If you find exculpatory evidence, include it.

Your reputation and the integrity of the justice system depend on ethical behavior.

quizData.question: It is acceptable to omit a finding that does not support the client's case if it was outside the requested scope.
quizData.explanation: You have a duty to report all relevant findings, exculpatory or not. Selectively omitting is unethical and could be obstruction.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Maintain an Audit Trail

Keep a log of all analysis steps, tool runs, and manual checks. This serves as the raw data behind the report and can be used in court if challenged.
